newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian Moslem party meets to debate election.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian Moslem party meets to debate election.

text.p: Leaders of Indonesia's Moslem-backed party met on Thursday to decide whether they would accept the outcome of last week's general elections, in which the ruling Golkar swept to a record victory.
The spokesman for the minority United Development Party (PPP), Usamah Hisyami, said they would discuss allegations of vote-rigging and that a statement would be made on Friday.
The PPP won just under 23 percent of the vote after the most violent election campaign in three decades.

Most of the violence involved supporters of the PPP and Golkar, whose victory was never in doubt. Financial markets were keeping a wary eye on the PPP meeting in case a rejection of the poll results produced further trouble.

Political analysts attributed some of the violence to the wealth gap, frustration over a carefully orchestrated and autocratic political system, and anger over pervasive corruption -- a campaign theme of the PPP.
"The meeting will...concentrate on discussing reports from the party's branches on election rigging. We need more time to discuss such issues," Hisyami said.
"We plan to issue a statement tomorrow (Friday) because we have decided to extend our high-ranking officials meeting to two days," he told Reuters.

The only other party legally entitled to contest the elections, the fragmented Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), took just three percent of the vote last week and has also charged that there were campaign and election irregularities.
In the last elections in 1992, Golkar got 68 percent of the vote, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.

The electoral commission held an unprecedented re-vote on Madura island off East Java on Wednesday after angry PPP supporters rioted and burned ballot boxes following the May 29 poll on reports that Golkar had swept up the vote in what was regarded as a PPP stronghold.

Reuters correspondent Jim Della-Giacoma reported from the Sampang regency on Madura that many PPP supporters had stayed away from the second poll, in which Golkar took about 58 percent of the vote from the 65 polling stations involved. The PPP got just over 41 percent and the PDI less than one percent.
The government had increased security on the strongly Moslem island and there were no signs of trouble after the re-vote in the coastal city of about 100,000 people.
Last week's vote was for 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives. The remaining 75 seats are filled by the military, which does not vote.

Indonesia is now looking ahead to a presidential election in March next year in which President Suharto, the world's second longest serving leader after Cuba's Fidel Castro, is expected to seek a seventh consecutive five-year term.
Suharto celebrates his 76th birthday on Sunday and there is keen interest as to who he will select as a vice-presidential running mate and potential successor, given his age.
